canonical.match_title: Our Lady of Medjugorje (Queen of Peace)

pages.student_title: Our Lady of Medjugorje, Queen of Peace
pages.subtitle: Since 1981, millions of people have come to a small village to pray, and the Church sees the good fruit of their prayer.

quick_facts.label: Who saw her
quick_facts.value: Six young people from the village, who say they still see her

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Devotion allowed (2024); the apparitions are not confirmed

pages.intro: In June 1981, six young people in the village of Medjugorje said they saw Mary on a hill. They said she called herself the Queen of Peace and asked for prayer, fasting, and peace. Since then, millions of people have come there to pray. The Church has not said that Mary really appeared, but it recognizes the many graces and the renewed faith that have come from Medjugorje.
story_paragraphs: Medjugorje is a small village in the mountains of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a country in southeastern Europe. Its parish church is named for Saint James.

On June 24 and 25, 1981, six young people from the village said they saw a beautiful lady on a rocky hill called Podbrdo. They said she was Mary, the Mother of Jesus. Their names are Marija, Ivan, Vicka, Jakov, Mirjana, and Ivanka. Today, they are grown-ups.

The young people said Mary called herself the Queen of Peace. They said she asked people to pray every day, to pray the Rosary, to fast, to read the Bible, to go to Confession, and to go to Mass. Peace, they said, begins in each person's heart and comes through prayer.
The six say that Mary has kept appearing to them, and that some of them still see her often. Many messages have been shared over the years.

News of Medjugorje spread around the world. About 40 million people have come there to pray. Many have gone to Confession for the first time in years. Many families have made peace. Some young people have decided to become priests or religious sisters.

For many years, the Church studied Medjugorje carefully. In 2024, with the approval of Pope Francis, the Vatican wrote a document called "The Queen of Peace." It said that the Church sees "abundant conversions" and "a frequent return to the sacraments" at Medjugorje. It said Catholics may pray there and be encouraged in their faith.

But the Church did not say that Mary really appeared. That question is still open. The Church reminds pilgrims that they come to Medjugorje to meet Mary, the Queen of Peace, and her Son, not to meet the people who say they see her.

pages.student_title: The Eucharistic Miracle of Bolsena and Orvieto
pages.subtitle: A priest who doubted, a host that bled, and the beginning of the feast of Corpus Christi.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: Blood was reported to flow from the host onto the altar cloth

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: Orvieto Cathedral and the Church of Saint Christina in Bolsena

pages.intro: In 1263, a priest on his way to Rome stopped in the town of Bolsena, Italy, to celebrate Mass. He had doubts about whether Jesus is truly present in the Eucharist. According to tradition, when he said the words of consecration, blood began to flow from the host. The next year, the Pope began the feast of Corpus Christi, which honors the Body of Christ.
story_paragraphs: Long ago, pilgrims traveling to Rome often stopped in Bolsena, a small town by a lake in Italy. In 1263, a priest named Peter, who was said to come from Prague, stopped there. He was praying for stronger faith. He struggled to believe that the bread and wine at Mass truly become the Body and Blood of Jesus.

Peter celebrated Mass in the church of Saint Christina, near her tomb. According to tradition, when he said the words of consecration, blood began to flow from the host. It fell onto his hands, onto the white linen cloth on the altar called the corporal, and onto the stone floor.

Pope Urban IV was staying in the nearby city of Orvieto. Peter went to him and told him what had happened. The Pope sent a bishop to Bolsena to look into it. The host and the bloodstained cloth were carried to Orvieto, where they were shown to the people.

The next year, in 1264, Pope Urban IV declared a new feast for the whole Church: the Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, also called Corpus Christi. The Pope asked a great teacher, Saint Thomas Aquinas, to write the prayers and songs for this feast. Some of his hymns, like the "Tantum Ergo," are still sung today when Jesus in the Eucharist is adored.
The oldest written account of the miracle that we have comes from Orvieto in the early 1300s, many years after 1263.

Today, the corporal is kept in the cathedral of Orvieto. The stones from the altar are still in the church of Saint Christina in Bolsena. Every year on Corpus Christi, Catholics around the world remember that Jesus is truly present in the Eucharist.

pages.subtitle: Hosts stolen in 1730 were found three days later, and they have stayed fresh for almost 300 years.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: Stolen hosts were found, and they have not spoiled for almost 300 years

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: The Basilica of Saint Francis in Siena

pages.intro: In 1730, thieves stole a silver container full of consecrated hosts from a church in Siena, Italy. Three days later, the hosts were found in a church collection box, dusty but whole. The friars kept them to honor them instead of giving them out at Communion. Bread usually spoils quickly, but these hosts have stayed fresh for almost 300 years.
story_paragraphs: Siena is an old city in Italy. On August 14, 1730, the night before the feast of the Assumption of Mary, most of the people of Siena were praying at the cathedral. The Basilica of Saint Francis was almost empty.
During that time, thieves crept into the basilica. They opened the tabernacle and stole the ciborium, a silver container holding hundreds of consecrated hosts. The people of Siena were heartbroken.

Three days later, on August 17, a priest in another church in Siena, Saint Mary of Provenzano, noticed something white in the collection box. Inside were the stolen hosts. They were dusty and some were tangled in cobwebs, but they were all there.

The hosts were carried back to the Basilica of Saint Francis. The friars decided not to give them out at Communion. Instead, they kept them so people could honor Jesus in them. They expected the hosts to crumble and spoil over time, as bread does.

But they did not spoil. Fifty years later, in 1780, a priest tasted one and found that it was still fresh. Later, in 1789, a bishop sealed some ordinary, unconsecrated hosts in a box to compare. Ten years later, those hosts had rotted away, while the hosts of 1730 were still whole.

In 1914, Pope Pius X allowed a team of scientists to study the hosts. They found that the hosts were made of ordinary flour and had not been specially treated. They could not explain why they had not spoiled.
In 1980, Pope John Paul II knelt before the hosts in Siena. He said, "This is the Presence!" Today, 223 of the hosts are still kept in the Basilica of Saint Francis.

pages.subtitle: A priest carried the Eucharist carelessly in his prayer book, and the pages were stained with blood.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: Near Siena, Italy; the relic is in Cascia

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A host was reported to bleed onto the pages of a prayer book

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: The Basilica of Saint Rita in Cascia

pages.intro: In 1330, a priest in Italy was called to bring Holy Communion to a man who was very sick. Instead of carrying the host in a special container, he tucked it between the pages of his prayer book. When he opened the book, according to the story, the host had bled and stained the pages. One of those pages is kept today in the basilica of Saint Rita in Cascia.
story_paragraphs: In the year 1330, near the city of Siena in Italy, a farmer was very sick. He asked for a priest to come and bring him Holy Communion.
When a priest brings Communion to someone at home, he usually carries the consecrated host in a small gold case called a pyx. This shows great respect for Jesus in the Eucharist.

But this priest did not use a pyx. Instead, he slipped the host between two pages of his breviary, the book of prayers that priests pray every day. Then he set off down the road to the sick man's home, carrying the book with him.
At the farmer's home, the priest heard the man's confession and forgave his sins in God's name. Then he opened his breviary to take out the host and give the man Communion.

According to the story, the priest was amazed. The host had begun to bleed, and it had stained both pages of the book with blood. The priest was sorry that he had not treated the Eucharist with more care.

The stained pages were kept with great care, and people came to honor them as a sign of Jesus' presence. One of them is now in the town of Cascia, in the basilica of Saint Rita. The miracle happened about fifty years before Saint Rita was born.

For hundreds of years, people have come to pray before this small, old page. The story of Cascia reminds us that the Eucharist is not ordinary bread. It is Jesus himself, and he should always be treated with love and respect.

pages.subtitle: In 2008, in a small town in Poland, a red mark appeared on a host that had fallen during Communion.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A red mark was reported on a host that had been placed in water

pages.intro: In October 2008, during Communion at Mass in Sokółka, Poland, a consecrated host fell to the floor. The priest placed it in water to dissolve, as the Church directs. A week later, a red mark was found on the host. The archbishop asked scientists and a Church commission to study what happened, and the host is now honored by the people of Sokółka.
story_paragraphs: Sokółka is a small town in the northeast of Poland. On October 12, 2008, during Communion at Mass, a consecrated host fell from the priest's hands onto the floor.

When a host falls and cannot be received, the Church asks the priest to place it in water until it dissolves. The priest picked up the host and put it in a small container of water. He placed it in the tabernacle. After Mass, the container was moved to a safe in the sacristy.
Seven days later, the safe was opened. Inside, the people saw that the host had not dissolved. Instead, there was a red mark on it.
The archbishop of the area, Edward Ozorowski, was told. In January 2009, he asked two doctors from the medical university in the nearby city of Białystok to study a tiny piece of the red mark.

The two doctors reported that the sample looked most like heart muscle. Other people disagreed and suggested that the red color might come from a kind of bacteria. The doctors said they did not agree with that idea.

The archbishop also set up a Church commission. It talked with the people who had been there and checked whether anyone had tampered with the host. It found no sign that anyone had. The case was then sent on to the Vatican's representative in Poland.

Today, the host is kept in the parish church in Sokółka, and people come to pray before it. But the most important thing is not the red mark. It is the faith that Jesus is truly present in every host, at every Mass, in every church in the world.

pages.subtitle: On Christmas Day in 2013, a host that fell during Communion was found with a red mark, and the Church studied it carefully.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A red mark was reported on a host that had been placed in water

pages.intro: On Christmas Day in 2013, at Saint Hyacinth's Church in Legnica, Poland, a consecrated host fell to the floor during Communion. It was placed in water, as the Church directs. A few days later, a red mark appeared on it. The bishop asked scientists and theologians to study it. In 2016, after asking the Vatican, he allowed the host to be honored.
story_paragraphs: Legnica is a city in the southwest of Poland. On December 25, 2013, Christmas Day, people were receiving Communion at Saint Hyacinth's Church. A consecrated host fell to the floor.
The priest followed what the Church asks in such cases. He picked up the host and placed it in a container of water, so it would dissolve. Then he put the container in the tabernacle.
In early January 2014, the priests checked on it. The host had not dissolved. A red mark now covered about one fifth of it.

Bishop Stefan Cichy, the bishop of Legnica at the time, set up a commission of scientists and theologians to study what had happened. Scientists took a tiny sample. Two laboratories studied it. They reported that it looked like pieces of human heart muscle.

In January 2016, the new bishop, Zbigniew Kiernikowski, sent the results to the Vatican office that studies such questions. The Vatican recommended that a suitable place be prepared for the host so that people could come to pray before it.

In April 2016, the bishop announced this to his people. He said he hoped it would "serve to deepen the cult of the Eucharist." That means he hoped it would help people love and honor Jesus in the Eucharist more.

The host is now kept at Saint Hyacinth's Church. People come to pray before it. But the bishop's hope reminds us what matters most: every host at every Mass is Jesus himself, whether or not anything unusual can be seen.

type_specific.what_catholics_believe: At every Mass, the priest says the words Jesus spoke at the Last Supper: "This is my body" and "This is my blood." Catholics believe that the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Jesus, even though they still look and taste like bread and wine. This is called the Real Presence.
type_specific.what_was_reported: a host that fell during Communion on Christmas Day 2013 did not dissolve in water, and a red mark appeared on it. Laboratories reported that a sample looked like heart muscle.
type_specific.what_the_church_says: after consulting the Vatican, the bishop allowed the host to be placed where people could honor it, hoping it would deepen love for the Eucharist. The Church never asks Catholics to believe in a particular miracle. What it teaches as true is that Jesus is really present in every Eucharist.
type_specific.evidence_note: The lab results were reported by the bishop and the scientists involved, but the full reports have not been widely published, and other experts have not studied the sample. We share what was reported without saying it proves the miracle.
